svg.title: P027. Average order value by state. Why each SQL step is needed.
svg.desc: Eight stages follow the same 49 orders. Blue columns come from Orders, green columns from Customers. The left join keeps order 11. The reporting label combines six missing state values with four stored Unknown values. Five groups become four qualifying states. Maharashtra averages 200 and Karnataka averages 100.
svg.text: From individual orders to average value by state
Which states have at least 10 orders, and which has the largest average basket?
49 orders → 49 joined orders → 5 state groups → 4 states with at least 10 orders

g.text: FROM Orders supplies one row per purchase, so every order and amount counts—even with missing customers or NULL amounts.
Orders 1–10 are the original sample. A range such as 1–5 represents five separate orders with identical values.
Order 11 records customer 99. The customer catalogue contains seven IDs and has no entry for 99.
Add Customers second to find the state for Orders.CustomerID. The LEFT JOIN keeps order 11 when the lookup fails.

g.aria-label: 49 orders → 49 joined rows · append the two customer columns
g.text: 49 orders → 49 joined rows · append the two customer columns
On order 11 the blue customer ID stays 99. Both green fields are NULL. Order 11 still has its amount of 50.

g.aria-label: Step 3. Why label the state before GROUP BY?
g.text: Why label the state before GROUP BY?
A missing customer, a missing state and a stored Unknown label belong to one reporting group. The CTE gives that group one key.

g.aria-label: 49 joined rows → 49 labeled rows · append the reporting state
g.text: 49 joined rows → 49 labeled rows · append the reporting state
Order 11, orders 22–26 and orders 27–30 all acquire the same state. In the outer query, state is this CTE column.

g.aria-label: Step 4. Why group by the displayed state?
g.text: Why group by the displayed state?
The requested grain is one row per reporting state. Put all orders with the same label together before checking the minimum.

g.aria-label: 49 labeled orders → 5 groups · exact members of each group
g.text: 49 labeled orders → 5 groups · exact members of each group
Unknown has 1 unmatched order + 5 with a missing state + 4 already labeled Unknown = 10. Grouping on the raw field would split

g.aria-label: Step 5. Why count buyers and orders separately?
g.text: Why count buyers and orders separately?
A customer can place several orders. Count distinct order-side customer IDs for buyers and every order ID for orders.

g.aria-label: 5 groups · count buyers and orders within each
g.text: 5 groups · count buyers and orders within each
Karnataka’s two customer IDs account for ten orders. Unknown has three buyers, including customer 99 from the order itself.

g.aria-label: Step 6. Why do SUM and AVG read only known amounts?
g.text: Why do SUM and AVG read only known amounts?
An order can exist while its amount is missing. SUM adds recorded amounts. AVG uses the number of recorded amounts as its

g.aria-label: 49 order rows · trace the amount cells for Maharashtra
g.text: 49 order rows · trace the amount cells for Maharashtra

g.aria-label: 5 state totals · Known amounts explains the AVG denominator
g.text: 5 state totals · Known amounts explains the AVG denominator
Maharashtra has five amounts of 200 and five NULLs. Its ten orders qualify and 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200. Kerala has zero known amounts.

g.aria-label: Step 7. Why use HAVING for the 10-order minimum?
g.text: Why use HAVING for the 10-order minimum?
Only a grouped state has an order count. Apply the cutoff to all orders in that group after calculating its measures.
Goa drops at nine orders, even with an AOV of 300. Kerala’s ten orders qualify even though its order value and AOV are NULL.

g.aria-label: Step 8. Why sort by average order value?
g.text: Why sort by average order value?
The marketing team wants states with the largest average basket first. Sorting the qualifying groups keeps their counts and totals

g.aria-label: 4 qualifying states → 4 final rows · the five requested output columns
g.text: 4 qualifying states → 4 final rows · the five requested output columns
Maharashtra and Karnataka each total 1,000. Their averages, 200 and 100, determine their order. The report accounts for 49 − 9 =
